title: Steering by the Stars
objective: After this level you can explain how sailors navigated by the stars.
summary: Wayfinders steer by where stars rise and set. A star's height gives latitude; longitude needed a clock, until Harrison's H4.

cards.headline: Hawaiian navigators steer by about 220 stars kept in their heads.
cards.body: No compass, no clock. Navigator Nainoa Thompson memorizes where each star comes up out of the sea and where it goes down. So what can the stars tell a sailor, and what can't they?

cards.headline: A compass made of horizon
cards.body: The Hawaiian star compass, developed by Nainoa Thompson, divides the horizon into 32 houses: the places where the Sun, stars, Moon and planets rise and set. It isn't an object at all. It lives in the navigator's memory. Watch a known star rise in its house and you know your heading. Thompson learned wayfinding from Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Satawal in Micronesia.
cards.callout: 32 houses on the horizon, carried in memory

cards.headline: How high tells you how far
cards.body: Stars also give you latitude: how far north or south you are. European sailors used the height of the Sun or the pole star, measuring its angle above the horizon with an instrument such as a sextant. Wayfinders read the same clue. Sailing north toward Hawaiʻi, the Southern Cross sits lower each night, and at Hawaiʻi's latitude the gap between its top and bottom stars matches the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.

cards.headline: East and west needed a clock
cards.body: Longitude was the hard part: there's no natural starting line. But Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so each hour between your local time and home time means 15° of longitude. You just needed a clock that kept home time at sea, and pendulum clocks were useless on a rolling ship. Britain's 1714 Longitude Act offered rewards. John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker, built H4, trialled on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761. Where am I? First ask: what time is it at home?

mascot.line: The stars answer north and south for free. East and west cost Britain a prize and a very patient clockmaker.

questions.prompt: In the Hawaiian star compass, what are the 32 houses?

options.label: Horizon points where stars rise and set
Constellations directly overhead at midnight
options.rationale: The houses sit on the horizon, not overhead.

options.label: Islands drawn on a paper sea chart
options.rationale: It's a mental map of directions, not a chart.

options.label: The hours of a navigator's night watch

questions.explanation: The star compass divides the horizon into 32 houses, the bearings where the Sun, stars, Moon and planets rise and set.

questions.prompt: Why did finding longitude at sea depend on a clock that kept home time?

options.label: A clock points to magnetic north
Each hour between local and home time equals 15° east or west
Clocks measure a star's height above the horizon
options.rationale: That gives latitude, measured with a sextant.

options.label: Stars only rise when the clock strikes the hour
options.rationale: Stars rise whenever Earth's turn brings them up.

questions.explanation: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so every hour of difference between local time and home time is 15° of longitude.

questions.prompt: From Level 81, canoes sailed the long sea road from Tahiti to Hawaiʻi. Heading north, how can a wayfinder tell she has reached Hawaiʻi's latitude?

options.label: The Sun sets exactly due north of the canoe
options.rationale: The Sun never sets in the north.

options.label: The ocean swells stop moving under the canoe
options.rationale: Swells keep rolling; the clue is in the sky.

options.label: The Southern Cross climbs higher in the sky each night
The Southern Cross's two gaps become equal

questions.explanation: At Hawaiʻi's latitude, the gap between the Southern Cross's top and bottom stars equals the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.
